title: Oklahoma meteor crater formed nearly 100 million years later than scientists thought
excerpt: Zircon crystals reveal that a meteor struck Oklahoma nearly 100 million years later than believed, around the time of a major mass extinction.
content:
Zircon crystals reveal that a meteor struck Oklahoma nearly 100 million years later than believed, around the time of a major mass extinction.

Scientists had grouped a meteor crater buried under a small Oklahoma town with a burst of ancient impacts.

Some researchers have suggested that burst points to a ring of debris around Earth long ago.

New research suggests the crater doesn’t belong in that group. The strike seems to have come much later, close to a mass extinction that wiped out a huge share of ocean life.

The study was led by Elizabeth Catlos, an associate professor in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at The University of Texas at Austin.

Her team dated tiny crystals from the crater’s bedrock. They kept getting an age near 370 million years, not the 467 million years on record.

“No matter what technique we used, it was coming back to this younger signal,” said Catlos.

That makes the impact nearly 100 million years younger than believed.

The team is careful about what the new age means, though. They say the crater may record a strike near the time of that die-off. They don’t claim the strike caused it.

The old age came from fossil teeth

The Ames impact structure stretches roughly 10 miles across beneath the Oklahoma town, hidden under nearly two miles of sediment. Its fractured rocks also hold significant deposits of oil and gas.

Until now, the crater had been dated only by fossils found in it: the teeth of conodonts, small eel-like animals from the Ordovician.

Catlos said the teeth were likely already millions of years old when the asteroid hit, and probably just got jumbled into the mix and stayed preserved.

A fossil shows when an animal lived. It doesn’t show when an impact mixed its remains into new rock.

That older date mattered. Several major North American impacts have ages centered around 467.5 million years ago, a cluster known as the Ordovician Meteor Event.

So many craters date to that stretch that some researchers have proposed Earth once had a Saturn-like ring of asteroid debris. Ames was one of them.

Dating the zircon crystals

The team turned to zircon crystals, tough mineral grains that trap uranium as they form. That uranium slowly turns into lead at a steady rate, so the balance of the two works as a clock.

Daniel Stockli, dean of the Jackson School of Geosciences and a co-author of the study, said this method is the most accurate way to tell when events like this happened.

He added that the fine structure inside zircon can also record the pressure of an impact.

The researchers measured 37 spots on zircons from the part of the bedrock that the impact melted. The dates showed when the granite-like rock itself formed, about 1.4 billion years ago. The youngest grains told a different story.

Ten of the 11 youngest dates agreed with each other. Together they gave an age of 369.7 million years, give or take about 6 million.

Impact marks were rare

When an impact hits a zircon, the crystal re-forms in a telltale pattern that the right images can show.

The team worked with NASA on two kinds of imaging. One shows a crystal’s growth bands, and the other shows where its structure has bent or broken.

Most of the zircons were undamaged, including the youngest ones. But two carried clear impact marks: fine cracks where the crystal had shifted slightly, and strings of tiny grains cutting across its bands.

A second mineral, from six rock samples, was dated too. Its ages came out much later, at about 310 million and 250 million years.

Those match the times the crater was heated and its oil formed, so later heating likely reset that clock.

The new age falls near an extinction

The mass extinction in question, the Frasnian-Famennian event, happened about 372 million years ago. It was one of several mass extinctions in Earth’s past.

The team wrote that the crater’s age also lines up with other North American impacts from around then.

Catlos said a sharper timeline matters for understanding how Earth works.

It makes a difference, she noted, whether a die-off was driven by something from space or by forces inside the planet, such as a series of massive volcanic eruptions.

“With this research, we’re basically taking a major pawn out of the Ordovician Meteor Event and dumping it into the Frasnian-Famennian event, and saying, ‘This is where this impact belongs,'” Catlos said.

Checking the other craters

The uncertainty on the age spans about 12 million years. That leaves room for the strike to have come millions of years before or after the extinction, and matching dates don’t show that one caused the other.

“These small crystals allow us to go back in time and learn about the major changes to Earth’s ancient landscapes,” Stockli said.

“It would be great to do this for more of the meteor impact sites across the continent so we could get a more accurate timeline for these major events.”

Dating zircons from the other Ordovician craters could show whether those strikes really happened as close together as their current ages suggest.

For now, Ames is out of the Ordovician count, and the other craters’ ages still stand.

The full study was published in the journal Meteoritics & Planetary Science.
